A 55-year-old woman comes to the emergency department reporting progressive muscle weakness
over the past 2 weeks, primarily affecting her lower extremities. She also notes increased urinary
frequency. One month ago, she was diagnosed with calcium phosphate kidney stones. Her medical
history includes rheumatoid arthritis, treated with methotrexate for 10 years, and type 2 diabetes
mellitus, managed with metformin. Vital signs are as follows: temperature 97.7°F (37°C), blood
pressure 148/98 mmHg, pulse 76/min, and respirations 14/min. Physical examination reveals mild
tenderness of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and 4/5 strength in the
lower extremities. Laboratory results are as follows: **Serum:** Na+: 137 mEq/L Cl-: 106 mEq/L K+:
2.9 mEq/L HCO3-: 18 mEq/L Glucose: 115 mg/dL Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL **Urine pH:** 5.6 What is the
most appropriate next step in this patient’s management? Answer Choices: (A) Begin oral sodium
citrate supplementation (B) Administer hydrochlorothiazide (C) Administer intravenous magnesium
sulfate (D) Initiate furosemide therapy (E) Start intravenous calcium gluconate (F) Start acetazolamide
therapy (G) Begin potassium replacement therapy with dextrose (H) Administer intravenous sodium
bicarbonate (I) Discontinue metformin immediately (J) Begin oral phosphate supplementation
 A. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate
B. Begin oral sodium citrate supplementation
C. Begin potassium replacement therapy with dextrose
D. Start acetazolamide therapy

E. Administer hydrochlorothiazide
F. Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate
G. Begin oral phosphate supplementation
